newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to mull tougher laws on sex discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Japan to mull tougher laws on sex discrimination.

text.p: A Japanese Labour Ministry panel called on Tuesday for a toothless equal opportunities law to to tightened to prevent discrimination against women, and for the repeal of a law preventing women working at night.

The proposed changes, which labour analysts said would close a 20-30 year gap between Japanese and Western gender equality policies, will be presented to parliament next month for implementation as early as 1998, ministry sources said.

The ministry's Council on Women's and Young Workers' Problems urged Labour Minister Yutaka Okano to add teeth to the 1986 Equal Employment Opportunity Law to curb discrimination against women in job advertisements, hiring and promotion.

The current law, which urges "efforts to protect the rights of female workers" but carries no punishment for offenders, should be revised to allow the labour minister to make public the name of the company as a punitive measure, the council said.
Regulations on sexual harassment should be included in the Equal Employment Opportunity Law and companies should be obliged to take preventative steps against such abuses, the council said.
In a more controversial change, the council called for lifting Labour Standards Law restrictions on overtime and late-night work by women.
The restrictions made it illegal for women outside of specialised professions such as nursing and broadcasting to work past 10 p.m. and limited their annual overtime hours to 150.
Proponents of the change, including manufacturers and the service industry, say the move would open a wider variety of jobs to women.
But opponents, including some labour unions and feminist groups, have warned that it will force upon women the same crushing work hours as Japanese men, who work among the longest hours in the world.
The lifting of overtime restrictions would also add to the burdens of working women who are also homemakers, opponents have said.
A Japan Confederation of Trade Unions survey of housework this year showed married women do an average of three hours and 10 minutes of housework per day, while their husbands do only 34 minutes.

Last Friday, Japan's cabinet adopted an action plan designed to curb sexual harassment, sexual violence and practices which discriminate against women. The plan called for a review of the 1986 equal opportunities law.
